title: Enheduanna
wiki_lead:
Enheduanna (Sumerian: 𒂗𒃶𒌌𒀭𒈾 Enḫéduanna, also transliterated as Enheduana, En-he2-du7-an-na, or variants; fl. c. 2300 BCE) was the entu (high) priestess of the moon god Nanna (Sīn) in the Sumerian city-state of Ur in the reign of her father, Sargon of Akkad (r. c. 2334 – c. 2279 BCE). She was likely appointed by her father as the leader of the religious group at Ur to cement ties between the Akkadian religion of her father and the native Sumerian religion. Enheduanna has been celebrated as the earliest known named author in world history.
A number of works in Sumerian literature, such as the Exaltation of Inanna feature her as the first-person narrator, and other works, such as the Sumerian Temple Hymns may identify her as their author. However, there is considerable debate among modern Assyriologists based on linguistic and archaeological grounds as to whether or not she actually wrote or composed any of the rediscovered works that have been attributed to her. Additionally, the only manuscripts of the works attributed to her were written by scribes in the First Babylonian Empire six centuries after she lived, written in a more recent dialect of the Sumerian language than she would have spoken. These scribes may have attributed these works to her as part of the legendary narratives of the dynasty of Sargon of Akkad in later Babylonian traditions.
The cultural memory of Enheduanna and the works attributed to her were lost some time after the end of the First Babylonian Empire. Her existence was first rediscovered by modern archaeology in 1927, when Sir Leonard Woolley excavated the Giparu in the ancient city of Ur and found an alabaster disk with her name, association with Sargon of Akkad, and occupation inscribed on the reverse. References to her name were then later discovered in excavated works of Sumerian literature, which initiated investigation into her potential authorship of those works. Enheduanna's archaeological rediscovery has attracted a considerable amount of attention and scholarly debate in modern times related to her potential attribution as the first known named author. She has also received considerable attention in feminism, and the works attributed to her have also been studied as an early progenitor of classical rhetoric. English translations of her works have inspired a number of literary adaptations and representations.

Enheduanna (Sumerian: 𒂗𒃶𒌌𒀭𒈾 Enḫéduanna, also transliterated as Enheduana, En-he2-du7-an-na, or variants; fl. c. 2300 BCE) was the entu (high) priestess of the moon god Nanna (Sīn) in the Sumerian city-state of Ur in the reign of her father, Sargon of Akkad (r. c. 2334 – c. 2279 BCE). These scribes may have attributed these works to her as part of the legendary narratives of the dynasty of Sargon of Akkad in later Babylonian traditions.
The cultural memory of Enheduanna and the works attributed to her were lost some time after the end of the First Babylonian Empire. Her existence was first rediscovered by modern archaeology in 1927, when Sir Leonard Woolley excavated the Giparu in the ancient city of Ur and found an alabaster disk with her name, association with Sargon of Akkad, and occupation inscribed on the reverse. References to her name were then later discovered in excavated works of Sumerian literature, which initiated investigation into her potential authorship of those works. Enheduanna's archaeological rediscovery has attracted a considerable amount of attention and scholarly debate in modern times related to her potential attribution as the first known named author. She has also received considerable attention in feminism, and the works attributed to her have also been studied as an early progenitor of classical rhetoric. English translations of her works have inspired a number of literary adaptations and representations.


Life


Sources
A few documents from her lifetime attest that Enheduanna was an historical person. The main one is a fragmentary disk with a partially erased inscription in her name (but known in its entirety thanks to a 19th or 18th century BC copy) and a relief probably representing her. She is absent from the administrative documentation of her time, but two cylinder seals, along with the impression of a third one found on a sealing unearthed at Ur, belong to some of her attendants.


A Princess from Akkad

Enheduanna's father was Sargon of Akkad, founder of the Akkadian Empire, a ruler whose reign is estimated to have lasted from approximately 2334 (or 2316) to 2279/2277 BC. Sargon was a figure of obscure origins, king of the city of Akkad, that had been of no significance until then and whose precise location remains unknown: likely on the Tigris, in central Mesopotamia, between present-day Samarra and Baghdad. Around 2300 BC, he conquered the land of Sumer and succeeded in bringing all of Lower Mesopotamia under his control, something no other king had ever done before him. He then unified a group of independent city-states, transforming them into provinces. He subsequently launched military campaigns that took him farther than his predecessors: as far as central Syria, into the Zagros Mountains, and into the eastern land of Elam. He was thus an extraordinary figure who attained the status of a major figure in ancient Mesopotamia, somewhat akin to Alexander the Great in the Greco-Roman world. The inscriptions concerning Enheduanna indicate her relationship to the ruler, since she is referred to as the “daughter of Sargon.”
Sargon’s family—and thus Enheduanna’s—can be reconstructed from contemporary sources. Sargon’s wife was a woman named Tashlultum, who would thus be Enheduana’s mother (there is no indication that the kings of Akkad were polygamous, although the possibility remains). Of Sargon’s five known children, she is therefore the only daughter. Two of Sargon’s sons—and thus Enheduanna’s brothers—Rimush and Manishtushu, succeeded their father (in an uncertain order) for about twenty years. Two other brothers of Enheduanna are known from inscriptions: Su-Enlil and Ilaba'is-takal. If the hymns attributed to her are to be believed, Enheduanna was likely still alive at the beginning of the reign of the dynasty’s fourth ruler, her nephew Naram-Sin (son of Manishtushu, reigned c. 2261–2206 or 2253–2198 BC), and was involved in the events of the great rebellion that engulfed Lower Mesopotamia at an unspecified time during his reign (see below).
The hymns attributed to her could reflect the political and ideological context of the time: Enheduanna would have composed them to support the dynasty through theology. It has been suggested that she was involved in a theological innovation aimed at integrating the pantheons of the Akkadian tradition with those of the Sumerian tradition, in order to strengthen the unity of the lands ruled by the Akkadian dynasty. This would primarily involve the assimilation of the Sumerian Inanna into the Akkadian Ishtar. However, there is insufficient evidence to support the existence of such a project. The Temple Hymns, which survey the sanctuaries of the major cities conquered and unified into a single state by Sargon, may have been intended to promote the unity of the kingdom through religion. The connection between Enheduanna and the goddess Inanna/Ishtar, as expressed in the hymns she is said to have written to praise her as the greatest deity, takes on its full meaning when viewed within the ideological context of the Akkadian period, since the Sargonic dynasty regularly placed itself under the auspices of the goddess.


Appointment as Priestess of Ur

At some unspecified time, her father (or one of her brothers) appointed her high priestess of Nanna, the Moon God (Sin in Akkadian), tutelary deity of the city of Ur. This position bears the Sumerian name en (enum in Akkadian), which, however, is not attested for Enheduanna’s time. It was the most important position within the hierarchy of the Sumerian clergy, often carrying heavy political weight..
It is not certain that this position existed in earlier periods. It may have been created by Sargon. It is, however, possible that this position was already held by women of royal rank. In any case, it is certain that other daughters of kings succeeded Enheduanna, beginning with her own grandniece, the daughter of Naram-Sin named Enmenanna. During the Third Dynasty of Ur (21st century BC), several princesses in turn attained this position,, and again during the subsequent Isin-Larsa period (19th-18th century BC). In the 6th century BC, King Nabonidus of Babylon revived this tradition several centuries after it had fallen into disuse, appointing his daughter Ennigaldi-Nanna.
It is likely that this high priestesses, who bear similar names beginning with en (meaning “high-priestess” or “lord”) and often ending with an (meaning “Heaven”; which can also refer to the god An), were given a new name upon assuming their office. "Enheduanna" would therefore not have been the princess’s birth name. Enheduanna's name is usually translated as "The high-priestess is the Ornament of Heaven." "Ornament of Heaven" (he2-du7-an-na) is also an epithet of Nanna.
Other known cases from the Akkadian period (and the Third Dynasty of Ur) show that high priestesses were chosen through an oracular procedure, as was usually the case for major liturgical offices.
Enheduanna was probably installed in the building within the god Nanna’s sanctuary known as the Giparu, since this is where the high priestesses of the god Nanna resided in later periods (and where her alabaster disk was found). But its levels of the Akkadian period could not be investigated during excavations, as it underwent significant alterations in subsequent periods.


The Disk of Enheduanna

The main source regarding Enheduanna’s role as high priestess of the god Nanna is an alabaster disk, 25.6 cm in diameter and 7 cm thick, unearthed at Ur in the Giparu. It features a bas-relief and an inscription on the reverse; although the latter is largely erased, it can be reconstructed thanks to a copy made on a tablet in the 19th century BC (assuming that copy indeed corresponds to this object). It was discovered 1927, as part of excavations at Ur directed by the British archaeologist Sir Leonard Woolley, shattered into several pieces, which has since been heavily (fancifully?) restored.
The bas-relief consists of a central frieze depicting a priestess accompanied by three male figures.Irene Winter states that "given the placement and attention to detail" of the central figure, "she has been identified as Enheduanna". She is depicted wearing a fringed tunic and a turban. The figure on the far left is a naked priest (possibly the one referred to in texts by the title lagar), who is pouring a libation onto an altar—an element largely worn away on the disk. The priestess is followed by two other, poorly preserved figures—likely officiating assistants—holding objects that resemble a musical instrument and a vessel (the one farthest right might be entirely a modern 'restoration'). A stepped structure, sometimes identified as a ziggurat, appears on the left side of the scene. 
The inscription (incorporating reconstructions based on a copy tablet) reads: "Enheduana, the zirru-priestess of Nanna, spouse of Nanna, daughter of Sargon, King of the World (or "of Kish"), built a pedestal in the temple of Inanna-ZAZA and named it: 'dais, table of Heaven (or "the god An").'"
Inanna-ZAZA is an aspect of the goddess Inanna/Ishtar that, apart from this instance, is known only from Mari in Syria. The mention of the goddess, instead of the god Nanna, finds an echo in the hymns to Inanna attributed to Enheduanna: it seems that her personal devotion was directed more toward this goddess (regarded as the protector of the Akkadian dynasty) than toward her divine spouse.
The disc is now a major artifact in the Middle East Galleries at the Penn Museum. Museum staff have shown the disc to the museum's special guests, such as Neil Gaiman. Together with other items related to the priestess, it went on display for the 2022-2023 exhibit centered on her, She Who Wrote: Enheduanna and Women of Mesopotamia.


Religious Role
The image and the text of the disk provide several essential pieces of information regarding the role of the high priestess of the god Nanna: she is considered his terrestrial spouse (dam), with the (Akkadian) title zirru being used as an epithet for his divine wife, the goddess Ningal.
On the other hand, there is no indication on the disk that she plays an active role in the ritual, as she is not the one performing the libation. Hymns attributed to Enheduanna, along with other sources concerning the high priestesses of Nanna from later periods, indicate that they participated in rituals. Their appointment in office was marked by an ordination ritual, a rite of passage signifying their entry into the sanctuary. The hymns to Nanna that mention Enheduanna may have been texts composed for this very occasion. They refer to purification rites and an enthronement through which she became the god’s earthly wife.. 
Once in office, a high priestess would participate in the management and maintenance of the sanctuary, as well as in routine cultic rituals, including those dedicated to the protection of the king. Her tenure involved ritual duties in the temple of Nanna and contributions to early Mesopotamian literature, marking her as a pivotal figure in the transition from Sumerian to Akkadian cultural dominance. Enheduanna is credited as the earliest known named author in history; no surviving texts from her lifetime bear her signature, but extant cuneiform manuscripts are later Old Babylonian copies (c. 2000â1600 BCE) that attribute authorship to her via colophons and employ first-person narration, though her direct authorship is debated. Key works attributed to her include the Exaltation of Inanna, a hymn praising the goddess Inanna (later Ishtar) and invoking Enheduanna's own restoration to power after a rebellion, and the Temple Hymns, a collection of 42 poems dedicated to various deities and sanctuaries. These compositions, copied and studied for centuries, demonstrate sophisticated poetic techniques and theological innovation, blending Sumerian and Akkadian elements to elevate Inanna's status. Her literary output not only preserved religious traditions but also supported imperial ideology, portraying divine favor for the Akkadian dynasty amid conquests and unrest. Archaeological evidence, such as the alabaster disk depicting her in ritual attire, corroborates her historical role, while textual records affirm her influence extended to successors who maintained the en-priestess office for generations. Enheduanna's legacy endures as a foundational voice in world literature, predating later figures like Homer by over a millennium.
